pensamiento:
The first requirement, QUS-001, has no role stated, so it doesn't pass and counts as a blocker. QUS-002 looks atomic at first glance, though it bundles a library update with removing TLS 1.1. Those could be read as one security change, so I'm leaning toward a qualified pass and still need to decide whether to flag it.

I'm checking the rest of the criteria against the requirement. QUS-004 seems to be missing a stated benefit, which I'll tie to INV-002 rather than flag separately so I don't over-flag. QUS-005 looks like a defect too, since the requirement names a specific library version and TLS 1.1 instead of describing the problem. QUS-006 and QUS-007 seem fine for now, though I still need to confirm there's no conflict with the other requirements.

I'm going through the remaining criteria: QUS-008 looks unique and fine, but QUS-009 is off because it lacks a role and breaks the usual "Como..." template, so I'll mark it as a minor issue. INV-001 seems independent, and INV-002 fails since no benefit is stated. INV-003 also fails because the scope is missing (which platforms, which library), so it can't be estimated. INV-004 looks small enough, and I still need to check INV-005 for verifiable criteria.

I'm checking the remaining rules now. The dependency question is still open: removing TLS 1.1 may depend on backend servers supporting TLS 1.2 or later, and I'm not sure that's stated clearly enough to call it a gap, so I'm leaning toward raising it as a question for the analyst. I'm also starting on DOR-002, where I need to see whether any rules are specific to a TLS version.

I'm checking the remaining DOR and BM criteria, and most of them don't seem to apply here: there are no monetary limits, no change to login or sessions, and nothing sensitive beyond the network security change. I'm treating DOR-002, DOR-003, BM-001 and BM-002 as not applicable for now.

I'm checking BM-005 through BM-007 against the requirement: no monetary or data change, no screen to make accessible, and the lack of a defined error case when the TLS handshake fails is a likely gap, so I'll mark BM-007 as a major issue. BM-004 looks compliant since removing TLS 1.1 aligns with the security controls. Now I'm turning to BM-008 and whether the library change affects both iOS and Android.

Next I'm going through the banking-specific criteria. BM-008 probably doesn't apply, since the change is network-level and doesn't use device features like biometrics or notifications. BM-009 doesn't either, because no personal data is involved. I'm now checking BM-010, the SUGEF rule, to see whether the requirement changes how financial information is communicated to the client.

I'm wrapping up the criteria check and tallying the defects: QUS-001 and INV-005 are blockers, QUS-005 and QUS-009 are minor, and INV-002, INV-003, DOR-001 and BM-007 are major. I'm leaving QUS-004 off the list for now, since the missing benefit is already covered under INV-002.

I'm deciding that the defects found so far are enough to return the story, and that size estimation can wait until the defects are fixed. Next I'll look up the estimation scale and reference stories to see whether a small library upgrade with TLS 1.1 removal matches any of them.

I'm estimating this at 3 points, since it's a technical change with a scope I can't fully gauge. I'll note that the devolution comes with defects, each needing a recommendation. The refined story has to follow the "como…, quiero…, para…" form, but I don't know the role, so I won't invent one; the field is required if the story is accepted and can stay empty if it's returned.

I'm settling on 3 points, since the scope is only partly clear: the library update and the TLS 1.1 removal are described, but not in full. I'm listing the defects, QUS-001, QUS-005, QUS-009, INV-002, INV-003, INV-005, DOR-001 and BM-007, and writing a recommendation for each one of at most 600 characters.

recomendaciones.texto: Falta el rol y la acción en formato 'Como <rol>, quiero <acción>, para <beneficio>'. Indica quién se beneficia (p. ej. un cliente de la app o el equipo de plataforma móvil, según corresponda) y para qué se hace el cambio. No inventes el rol: confírmalo con el analista o el producto.

El enunciado impone la solución técnica (librería de red v5 y retiro de TLS 1.1). Describe el problema o la necesidad que motiva el cambio (p. ej. riesgo de seguridad en comunicaciones, incumplimiento de un requisito) y deja la solución técnica para los criterios de aceptación o notas.
La HU no sigue la plantilla 'Como…, quiero…, para…' que usa el resto del backlog. Reformúlala en esa plantilla una vez definido el rol y el beneficio.

No hay beneficio explícito (la parte 'para…'). Indica el valor para el usuario o el negocio, por ejemplo, la seguridad de las comunicaciones de la app o la compatibilidad con un requisito normativo. Debe tener valor para alguien distinto del equipo de desarrollo.

Falta información para estimar el alcance: plataformas afectadas (iOS, Android o ambas), versiones mínimas de sistema operativo, qué componentes de la app usan la librería, y si hay pruebas de regresión esperadas. Aporta estos datos o confirma que el alcance es toda la app.

No hay criterios de aceptación. Agrega reglas observables, por ejemplo: 'Si la app se conecta a un servicio que solo acepta TLS 1.1, la conexión falla y se muestra el mensaje definido'; 'La app negocia TLS 1.2 o superior en todas las conexiones'; 'La versión de la librería instalada es la 5.x'.

Identifica las dependencias: el cambio de TLS 1.1 puede requerir que los servicios del core y los proveedores externos soporten TLS 1.2 o superior. Nombra esos sistemas o equipos y confirma que están listos antes de retirar TLS 1.1.

No se define el comportamiento sin conexión ni los errores de conexión tras el cambio (por ejemplo, fallo de handshake TLS en dispositivos antiguos). Define qué ve el cliente y cómo se evita reintentar una operación monetaria en curso sin confirmar su estado.
